It is also said: it is that which makes a thing alive, and it is that by which one can come to know and have power. Death is the absence of that. [[Mahmud said: "That is, what makes a thing alive, or what makes perception valid by its existence, and death is the absence of that... etc." Ahmad said: He erred in explaining death. His habitual practice, well known, is to interpret, and the interpretation follows the opinions of the Qadariyah, among them the one whom God has cut off the mention of: that death is non-existence. This is a manifest error. The creed of the People of the Sunnah is that it is an existential matter that is opposed to life. How could non-existence be of this standing? If non-existence were a created, originated thing, and the non-existence of originated things were established from eternity, it would follow that the originated things are cut off from eternity, and that is more absurd than saying the world is eternal. So look at where this desire leads, and how it casts its follower down and destroys him. We seek refuge in Allah from slips and errors.]] Regarding it: the meaning of God creating death and life is bringing into existence that which makes it valid and annihilating it. The meaning is: He created your death and your life, O accountable ones, ﴿that He may test you﴾. He called the knowledge of what actually occurs from them by their choice a "test" (balwa), which is the experience, as a metaphor from the act of one who tests. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive﴾. If you ask: from where does the phrase ﴿which of you is best in deeds﴾ relate to the verb of testing? [[Mahmud said: "From where does His saying 'which of you is best in deeds' relate to the verb of testing? Ta'liq is when after it you place something that fills the place of both objects together, as in your saying, "I knew which of them is Amr," and "I knew whether Zayd is going." Do you not see that after one object has preceded, there is no difference between what follows being introduced with an interrogative particle and what is not introduced with it? Had it been ta'liq, the two situations would have differed, as they differ in your saying, "I knew whether Zayd is going," and "I knew Zayd going."

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the Overpowering, whom none who does evil can escape, ﴿the Forgiving﴾ to whoever repents of wrongdoing.

This is a description by the verbal noun, or it means "possessors of layers," or "they were made into layers." ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Gracious no discrepancy (tafāwut)﴾. It is also read as "tafawwut." The two forms have the same meaning, like their saying "tazāharū min nisā'ihim" and "tazahharū," and "ta'āhadtuhu" and "ta'ahhadtuhu." From it comes their saying: "a disproportionate creation," and its opposite: "proportionate." If you ask: how does this clause relate to what precedes it? I say: it is a descriptive clause accompanying His saying "ṭibāqan," and its original form is: "you see in them no discrepancy." It is the plural of "fatr," which is a split; it is said: "fatarahu, fa-infatara" (he split it, and it split). From it: "fatara nāb al-ba'īr" (the camel's tooth split), as one says "shaqqa" and "bazala." Its meaning: the flesh split and emerged. He commanded him to repeat the gaze over them, scanning and tracing, seeking a flaw or defect. ﴿It will return to you (yanqalib ilayka)﴾: that is, if you return the gaze and repeat the look, your sight will not return to you with what you sought of seeing a defect and perceiving a fault; rather, it will return to you "khāsi'an" and "ḥasīran," that is, distanced from hitting its target. It is as if it is driven away from that with humiliation and abasement [[His saying "with humiliation and abasement" means smallness and disgrace, as in the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]], and with fatigue and weariness from prolonged circling and repetition. If you ask: how does the gaze return "khāsi'an ḥasīran" by returning twice? I say: the meaning of the dual here is repetition by multiplicity [[Mahmud said: "Why did he single out the two returns? He answered that the meaning of the dual here is multiplication..." Ahmad said: In His saying "yanqalib ilayka al-baṣar" the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. In it there is the benefit of alerting that what returns khāsi'an ḥasīran without perceiving the rifts is the instrument by which one seeks to perceive what exists; so when nothing is perceived, this shows that there is nothing. Of this kind is His saying, "He created seven heavens in layers; you see in the creation of the Most Gracious no discrepancy." Its original form is "you see in their creation any discrepancy," but He mentioned them as separated from the creation of the Most Gracious, as an alert to the reason which safeguarded them from rifts and discrepancy.]], as in your saying, "Labbayka wa-sa'dayka" (here I am at Your call, again and again), meaning many responses following one another, and as in their proverb: "Dahdarin Sa'd al-Qayn" [[His saying "dahdarin ... etc." In the Qamus, with both dals pronounced and the ra doubled: a name for a champion, and for falsehood and lying, like "al-dahdar." "Dahdarin Sa'd al-Qayn" means: O champion Sa'd the smith. Or it is said that a man claimed his name was Sa'd for a time, then his lie became clear, and it was said to him that. Or: "Ḍa" as a command from "al-dahā'," and "darin" from "dara," meaning he continued, i.e., exaggerated in lying, O Sa'd. There are other explanations, so refer to it; thus in the margin of the original. (ʿ)]] from this: that is, falsehood upon falsehood. If you ask: then what is the meaning of "thumma irji'" (then return)? I say: He commands the return of the gaze, then commands that he should not be satisfied with the first return and the foolish glance, but should pause after it and gather his gaze, then repeat and repeat, until his sight is worn out from the length of repetition, for he will find no trace of any rift.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the Overpowering, whom none who does evil can escape, ﴿the Forgiving﴾ to whoever repents of wrongdoing.

I say: the meaning of the dual here is repetition by multiplicity [[Mahmud said: "Why did he single out the two returns? He answered that the meaning of the dual here is multiplication..." Ahmad said: In His saying "yanqalib ilayka al-baṣar" the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 67, verses 16–19:

﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven?﴾ has two interpretations. The first: it refers to His dominion (malakut) in the heaven, because the heaven is the dwelling of His angels, and His Throne, His Footstool, and the Preserved Tablet are there, and from it His decrees, His books, and His commands and prohibitions descend. The second: they used to hold the belief of anthropomorphism (tashbih), that He is in the heaven, that mercy and punishment descend from Him, and they would call upon Him from that direction. So it was said to them, in accordance with their belief: "Are you secure from the One whom you claim to be in the heaven, though He is exalted above place, that He might cause you to be swallowed up by the earth or send against you a violent wind?" This is like when you say to one of the anthropomorphists: "Are you not afraid of the One above the Throne, that He may punish you for what you do, when you see him committing some sins?"

Or who is it that is pointed to, and it is said: "This is the one who provides for you, should He withhold His provision?" This is according to the supposition (of the question). It is also permissible that it refers to all the idols, because they believe that they protect (their worshippers) from calamities and that they are provided for by the blessing of their gods; so it is as if they were the helping soldier and the provider. A similar statement is His, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have gods who protect them from Us?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:43]. Rather, they persisted in arrogance and aversion, i.e., they went to excess in opposition and fled from the truth because it was heavy upon them, so they did not follow it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 67, verse 22–24:

He makes "akabba" (أكب) the intransitive counterpart (muṭāwaʿa) of "kabbahu" (كبه), as in: "I overturned him (kabbabtuhu), so he toppled (fa-akabba)," which is among the rare and anomalous forms. Similar to it is: "The wind scattered the clouds (qashaʿat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb), so they dispersed (fa-aqshaʿa)." But this is not the case, and no form of the pattern "af'ala" comes as a muṭāwaʿa; only the bearers of the Book of Sibawayh master this, and "akabba" is rather of the pattern of "infaḍḍa" and "alʾama" [[The phrase "min bāb infaḍḍa wa-alʾama": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "infaḍḍa al-qawm" means their wealth was destroyed; and "infaḍḍū" also means their provisions ran out, as in "irmalū." Also in it: "alʾama al-rajul" means the man did what drew people's condemnation upon him, becoming base. (ʿ)]]. Its meaning is: he entered into a state of prostration (al-kabb), and became one who is prostrate (dhākib). Likewise, "aqshaʿa al-saḥāb" means: the clouds entered into dispersal (al-qashʿ). The muṭāwaʿa of "kabba" and "qashaʿa" is:

"inkabba" and "inqashaʿa."

If you ask: what is the meaning of "yamshī mukkiban ʿalā wajhihi" (one who walks prone upon his face), and how does it contrast with "yamshī sawiyyan ʿalā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm" (one who walks upright on a straight path)? I say: its meaning is that he walks stumbling over a customary place that is not level, having dips and rises, so he trips every moment and falls prone on his face. Thus his condition is the opposite of the one who walks upright, i.e., standing, safe from stumbling and falling. Or it means one whose direction is level and who deviates little, unlike the one who stumbles, who swerves this way and that on a level road. It is also permissible that what is meant is the blind man who cannot find the way and so stumbles, and so keeps falling on his face, and that he is not like the upright, sound-sighted man walking on a road he is guided along. This is an example for the believer and the disbeliever. It is related from Qatada: the disbeliever is prone (akabb) to the disobediences of Allah the Exalted, so Allah will gather him on the Day of Resurrection upon his face. It is related from al-Kalbi: it refers to Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. And by "the upright one" is meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); and it was said: Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib.

The pronoun in *ra'awhu* refers to the promise (*al-wa'd*). *Zulfah* means nearness, and its accusative form is either a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) or an adverbial accusative (*ẓarf*), meaning: they saw it as near, or as a place that is near.

*Sī'at wujūh* means that the sight of the promise distressed their faces. Sadness was upon them, eclipse and dust (*qutra*) covered them, and they grimaced. The phrase *wa-kama yakūnu* is perhaps *kama* without the *wa*. (ع)

This is like the face of one who is led to execution or exposed to some torment.

And it is said by the speakers, the angels of punishment (*al-zabāniyya*): ﴿هَٰذَا الَّذِي كُنتُم بِهِ تَدَّعُونَ﴾ "This is what you used to call for."

*Tadda'ūn* is on the form *tafta'ilūn* from *du'ā'*, meaning you seek it and hasten toward it. It was also said that it is from *da'wā* (claim), meaning that because of it you used to claim that you would not be resurrected.

It is also read *tadda'ūn*.

The Meccan disbelievers used to invoke destruction upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and upon the believers, so he was commanded to say to them: "We are believers, awaiting one of the two good outcomes: either we perish as you wish, and then we return to Paradise; or we are shown mercy through victory and the ascendancy of Islam, as we hope. So what are you doing? Who will protect you, while you are disbelievers, from the punishment of the Fire? You cannot escape it." The meaning is: you seek for us a destruction which is in fact a hastening towards success and happiness, while you are in a matter which is a destruction with no destruction after it, and you are heedless, not seeking deliverance from it.

Or it may mean: if Allah destroys us by death, then who will protect you after the death of your guides and of those who hold you back from the Fire? And if He shows us mercy by granting us respite and dominance over you and slaying you, then who will protect you, for whoever is slain at our hands is lost. Or it may mean: if Allah destroys us in the Hereafter for our sins, although we are Muslims, then who will protect the disbelievers, who are more deserving of destruction because of their disbelief? And if He shows us mercy through faith, then who will protect one who has no faith?

If you ask: why was the object of *āmannā* (we believed) placed late, while the object of *tawakkalnā* (we put our trust) was placed early? I answer: *āmannā* came as an indirect allusion (*ta'rīḍ*, an oblique reference) to the disbelievers, since it came right after mention of them, as if it were said: "We believed and did not disbelieve as you did." Then he said: "In Him we put our trust," specifically: we did not rely on what you rely on, of your men and your wealth.

**ghawran** (sunken, gone deep into the earth). It is also said, on the authority of al-Kalbi, that it means it cannot be reached by buckets. It is a description using the **maṣdar** (verbal noun), like *ʿadl* (justice) and *riḍā* (contentment).

It is related that some of the **shuṭṭār** (roguish, libertine types) heard it recited in his presence and said: "Axes and hoes will bring it up," and the water of his eyes departed. We seek refuge in Allah from boldness toward Allah and toward His verses.

On the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mulk, it is as if he has given life to the Night of Power."¹

¹ Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh, on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).
